questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Digit-string counting under two simultaneous constraints with overlap
questions.stem: How many five-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1 to 9, with no digit repeated, that are BOTH even AND greater than 50000?
questions.explanation: The first digit must be in {5,6,7,8,9} (5 choices) and the last digit in {2,4,6,8} (4 choices), but they must be different digits. Ordered (first,last) pairs = 5*4 minus the two clashes (6-6 and 8-8) = 18. The three middle positions are any ordered arrangement of the remaining 7 digits: 7*6*5 = 210. Total = 18*210 = 3780. B=4200 = 5*4*210 forgets that the first and last digit cannot coincide. C=8400 drops the 'even' condition (5*8*7*6*5). D=6720 drops the 'greater than 50000' condition (last even, first any remaining: 4*8*210). E=3360 over-removes the overlap, subtracting 4 pairs instead of 2 (16*210).

questions.subject: biology
questions.skill: Deducing a parental genotype from test-cross ratios under epistasis
questions.stem: Flower colour in a plant depends on two independently assorting genes. Gene P is required for any colour: plants that are pp are white regardless of the second gene. In plants that carry at least one P allele, gene R sets the shade — R_ gives red and rr gives pink. A red-flowered plant of unknown genotype is test-crossed with a white plant of genotype pprr. The offspring appear in the ratio 1 red : 1 pink : 2 white. What is the genotype of the red parent?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The pprr parent contributes only 'p r' gametes, so each offspring's phenotype is set by the red parent's gamete: a p gamete gives a pp (white) offspring, a P gamete gives a coloured offspring that is red if the gamete carries R and pink if it carries r. A PpRr parent makes PR, Pr, pR, pr gametes in equal amounts, yielding PpRr (red), Pprr (pink), ppRr (white), pprr (white) = 1 red : 1 pink : 2 white, matching the data. B (PPRr) gives only P gametes, so no white offspring (ratio 1 red : 1 pink : 0 white). C (PpRR) never yields an rr offspring, so no pink (1 red : 0 pink : 1 white). D (PPRR) gives all red. E (Pprr) is a pink plant, not red, so it contradicts the stem, and it would produce no red offspring at all.

questions.subject: biology
questions.skill: Propagating carrier probability across generations and computing offspring risk
questions.stem: A condition is known to be inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. In the pedigree shown, squares are males and circles are females; a fully shaded symbol is affected, and open symbols are unaffected. Individual I-1 (an affected male) has a daughter, II-2, who married an unaffected man (II-1) from the general population. Their daughter, III-1, has now married an unaffected man (III-2), also from the general population. Assuming all individuals who marry into the family are unaffected and carry no copy of the disease allele, what is the probability that III-1 and III-2's first child will be an affected boy?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Because I-1 is an affected male (X^a Y), he gives his only X (bearing a) to every daughter, so II-2 is an obligate carrier (X^A X^a) with certainty. II-2 (carrier) x II-1 (X^A Y) gives daughters that are carriers with probability 1/2, so P(III-1 is a carrier) = 1/2. If III-1 IS a carrier, then crossed with an unaffected non-carrier man her children are 1/4 affected sons, 1/4 unaffected sons, 1/4 carrier daughters, 1/4 non-carrier daughters — so P(affected boy | III-1 carrier) = 1/4. Total = 1/2 x 1/4 = 1/8. B (1/4) forgets the 1/2 chance that III-1 is even a carrier, treating her as certain. C (1/2) treats every son of a carrier as affected. D (1/16) multiplies in an extra 1/2. E (0) wrongly assumes an affected male 'cannot transmit', ignoring transmission through obligate-carrier daughters.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.subtopic: Limiting reagent combined with gas stoichiometry
questions.skill: Limiting reagent, mole ratio, and PV = nRT together
questions.stem: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g). A 3.27 g piece of zinc is added to 50.0 mL of 1.50 M HCl and the reaction is allowed to go to completion. What is the maximum volume of H2 gas produced, measured at 27 C and 1.00 atm? (Zn = 65.4; R = 0.0821 L.atm.mol^-1.K^-1.)
questions.explanation: n(Zn) = 3.27/65.4 = 0.0500 mol; n(HCl) = 0.0500 L x 1.50 M = 0.0750 mol. Consuming 0.0500 mol Zn would need 0.100 mol HCl, but only 0.0750 mol is available, so HCl is limiting. n(H2) = 0.0750 x 1/2 = 0.0375 mol. V = nRT/P = 0.0375 x 0.0821 x 300 = 0.924 L. D: took Zn as limiting (0.0500 mol H2). E: used HCl as limiting but forgot the 1:2 HCl:H2 ratio (0.0750 mol H2). B: used the STP molar volume 22.4 L/mol despite the stated 27 C. A: failed to convert 27 C to 300 K.

questions.competency: Recognizing that meiosis is the reductional division producing haploid gametes in animals, distinguishing it from mitosis and asexual reproduction modes
questions.subject: biology
questions.skill: Distinguishing meiosis (reductional division) from mitosis using DNA content and chromosome number across cell states
questions.stem:
A researcher measures the DNA content (in arbitrary units, "au") of single nuclei taken from the gonad of an animal whose somatic cells have a diploid chromosome number of 2n = 8 and a G1 DNA content of 4 au. She sorts the nuclei into four categories, I–IV, summarized in the table:

Category — DNA content per nucleus — chromosome number per nucleus
I  — 8 au — 8
II — 4 au — 8
III — 4 au — 4
IV — 2 au — 4

Each nucleus belongs to a genuine cellular state that occurs somewhere along the pathway from a germ-line stem cell to a finished gamete. Which category corresponds to a cell that has completed the reductional division but has NOT yet completed the second division?

options.E: None of the categories, because the reductional division halves DNA content and chromosome number simultaneously

questions.explanation:
Anchor values: a G1 somatic/germ cell has 2n = 8 chromosomes and 4 au of DNA. After S phase (DNA replication) the cell still has 8 chromosomes but each is now two sister chromatids, so DNA doubles to 8 au — that is Category I (a primary spermatocyte/oocyte entering meiosis I). Meiosis I is the REDUCTIONAL division: it separates homologous chromosomes, halving the CHROMOSOME number from 8 to 4, but each chromosome still consists of two chromatids, so DNA per nucleus is 8/2 = 4 au. That state — 4 au, 4 chromosomes — is Category III, a secondary spermatocyte after meiosis I but before meiosis II. Meiosis II (equational) then separates sister chromatids, giving the gamete 4 chromosomes and 2 au — Category IV. Correct answer: C. 
Trap A (Category I, 8 au / 8 chromosomes): the post-S primary spermatocyte BEFORE meiosis I; picks the cell that is about to undergo, not one that has completed, the reductional division. 
Trap B (Category II, 4 au / 8 chromosomes): an impossible/decoy state (8 chromosomes but only 4 au) that a student invents by wrongly assuming meiosis I halves DNA while leaving chromosome number unchanged — the exact inversion of what reduction does. 
Trap D (Category IV, 2 au / 4 chromosomes): the finished gamete AFTER meiosis II; picks the end product, confusing "completed both divisions" with "completed only the first (reductional) division." 
Trap E: false premise — meiosis I halves chromosome number (8→4) but NOT DNA content per nucleus (stays 8→... actually 8 au before, and each of the 4 chromosomes retains 2 chromatids so total is 4 au — a halving of DNA too, but only because homologs, each 2 au, are separated). The key error E encodes is the belief that reduction cannot leave replicated (two-chromatid) chromosomes behind; in fact Category III exists precisely because sister chromatids are still joined after meiosis I.

questions.competency: Identifying tRNA as the adaptor molecule that delivers amino acids to the ribosome during translation, and distinguishing the functional roles of the major RNA classes (mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, snRNA, siRNA)
questions.subject: biology
questions.skill: Identifying tRNA as the adaptor molecule that delivers amino acids to the ribosome during translation, and distinguishing the functional roles of the major RNA classes (mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, snRNA, siRNA)
questions.stem: In a cell-free translation experiment, a researcher first charges a tRNA that has the anticodon 3'-UGG-5' with its correct amino acid, threonine. She then uses a chemical treatment that converts the already-attached threonine into alanine WITHOUT altering the tRNA's anticodon or its aminoacyl bond. This modified charged tRNA is added to a system translating an mRNA that contains the codon 5'-ACC-3' at a specific position. When the resulting protein is analysed, which amino acid is found at that position, and what does this outcome reveal about the molecule that determines it?

options.A: Alanine is inserted, because the ribosome selects the tRNA by its anticodon, and the residue actually added is whatever amino acid is currently attached to that tRNA
options.B: Threonine is inserted, because the ribosome proofreads each incoming amino acid against the codon and rejects any tRNA carrying the wrong residue
options.C: Alanine is inserted, because the mRNA codon is read directly by the amino acid, and the tRNA merely provides a scaffold with no role in selecting the residue
options.D: No amino acid is inserted, because a mismatch between the amino acid and the codon causes the ribosomal rRNA to stall and abort translation at that position
options.E: Threonine is inserted, because tRNA is only a passive carrier and the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase re-checks the pairing at the ribosome before the residue is added to the chain

questions.explanation: The codon 5'-ACC-3' pairs antiparallel with the anticodon 3'-UGG-5', so this specific tRNA is the one recruited at that position regardless of which amino acid it carries. Because the amino acid was chemically converted AFTER charging, the tRNA now bears alanine yet keeps its threonine-specifying anticodon. During elongation the ribosome selects the aminoacyl-tRNA purely by codon-anticodon base pairing and then transfers whatever residue is esterified to it, so ALANINE is inserted. This is the core of the adaptor hypothesis: tRNA is the informational adaptor and the ribosome does not read the chemical identity of the amino acid. (A) is correct. (B) encodes the misconception that the ribosome proofreads amino-acid identity against the codon; selection is by anticodon only, so it wrongly predicts threonine. (C) reaches the right amino acid but by a fatally wrong mechanism — it claims the amino acid reads the codon directly and denies tRNA any adaptor role, contradicting the whole experiment. (D) invents an rRNA-based abort step; rRNA catalyses peptide-bond formation and forms the ribosomal core but does not audit amino-acid/codon matching, so translation continues. (E) reflects the misconception that aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase re-inspects the tRNA at the ribosome; the synthetase acts only during charging and is not part of the elongation step, so it cannot correct the altered residue. The two wrong-amino-acid options (B, E) both falsely assume a downstream fidelity check on the residue itself, which does not exist.
